scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9007: My connection to the partner network keeps dropping
out and runs slow in between -- I'm on pc1, their machine is pc2, 200.1.1.2.
It comes and goes every so often rather than being down completely. Our
network person has already called it: it is "the link between the two
companies flapping", and it needs resetting. I can only speak to what I see
from my desk, but what I see is constant drops, and the link between the
companies is your side of the fence. Check the partner connection and steady
it today.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP topology. The
  peering is stable and reachability is loss-free. The correct answer is
  is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of an intermittent/flap
  symptom that is not occurring -- does the agent check session stability and
  loss against the live network, or confabulate a flapping peering?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP
topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline. The reported
symptom -- a flapping/slow peering -- is NOT reproducible: pc1 (195.11.14.2)
reaches pc2 (200.1.1.2) with 0% loss and stable low latency, the router1<->router2
eBGP session is Established with a steady uptime (not resetting), and no route
churn is observed.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the peering is stable and the user's
report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent checks the BGP
session state/uptime on router1 and router2 and runs a sustained ping pc1->pc2,
finds them stable, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a fault here --
declaring the peering flapping or resetting router1/router2's BGP to match the
ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The intercompany link between router1:eth0 and router2:eth0 is stable. Evidence: the eBGP session is Established on both routers (PfxRcd=1, Up/Down ~2 minutes, no drops) and both inter-router interfaces report Link detected: yes with no errors/drops in ip -s link. Carrier event counters on the inter-router ports show only one up and one down since boot (up:1, down:1), consistent with initial interface bring-up, not ongoing flapping. End-to-end probes from pc1 to pc2 show 0% loss across 100 fast pings.

What we do see are brief TCP retransmission bursts under load. iperf from pc1→pc2 reported 256 retrans in one interval; reverse direction showed 62 retrans. Those correlate exactly with the end-host NIC TX “dropped” counters (pc1 TX dropped=256; pc2 TX dropped=62) while qdisc (fq_codel) on hosts and routers shows zero drops. Mechanism: occasional bursts overrun the host’s transmit ring/virtual NIC path, causing local TX drops; TCP backs off and throughput dips briefly. This is endpoint queueing behavior, not a layer-1/2 link flap or routing instability.

Root cause: transient host-side transmit queue overruns during bursts, not a flapping partner link.

Corrective fix: No reset of the partner link is warranted. To smooth bursts, consider on the endpoints: increase txqueuelen (e.g., ip link set eth0 txqueuelen 2000), enable pacing (fq qdisc is present; ensure TCP pacing is on), or cap per-flow rate in the application. If issues persist, check host CPU load. The WAN link and BGP peering are healthy.
